lines: Thunder shook the map table so hard loose maps tried to fly, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked maps, compasses, and road marks after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the map table, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked the maps twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have maps to set right.
I checked dry parchment and map frames for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and <dark_gray><wavy>fear</wavy></dark_gray>.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the map table after.
The maps can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach around the map table, then stopped pretending things matter more than neighbors.
The smoke is thinning near the map table, but everyone is still sniffing the air like it might lie.
During a raid, maps can wait flat on the table. Who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands near the map table still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before maps, compasses, and road marks. That's the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the map table and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the map table, I saw fear cross the square. Then I saw courage get there first.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the map table first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the road past the last torch and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave the map table enough light to count wounds, missing blocks, and who made it home.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping a fresh mark on the map between us and teeth.
We are safe enough near the map table, though every shadow is being inspected twice.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning sand out of the compass case.
I checked maps, compasses, and road marks, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the map table, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
A hard wind teaches a cartographer which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough near the map table, though the whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
Maps can wait flat on the table. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the map table found shelter.
Cold works quietly around the map table. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing snow off the road signs and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now near the map table. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
